speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: CLOSING OF CERTAIN TRIBUTARIES OF SAINT JOHN RIVER TO GILL-NET FISHING
speechtext:
I should like to direct a question to whoever is acting Minister of Fisheries in the absence of that minister. The question is based on a report that the department has closed certain tributaries of the Saint John river to net fishing. This is the season of the year when people along the river fish for different kinds of fish, and I would ask the minister this question: Has the Department of Fisheries closed the Jemseg river and Raft channel to the Grand lake to all kinds of net fishing? If so, why has this been done? Will the department consider cancelling this order at once?

Supply-A gricultu re

speakeroldname: Hon. ALPHONSE FOURNIER (for the Minister of Fisheries):
subtopic: CLOSING OF CERTAIN TRIBUTARIES OF SAINT JOHN RIVER TO GILL-NET FISHING
speechtext:
In the absence of the Minister of Fisheries I received notice of the question which the hon. gentleman has asked. The answer to the first question is in the affirmative. As regards the second part of the question the answer is: As the Jemseg river is quite narrow, gill-nets, ostensibly set for the taking of shad, have been taking striped bass. At the request of the provincial authorities and of the New Brunswick fish and game protective association, as well as on the recommendation of the officers of the department, the use of gill-nets was prohibited in the Jemseg river, in order to facilitate the ascent of fish in the river, thereby providing better angling from which the province and the people along the river will derive greater benefit from tourists and anglers.
As to the third question-will the department consider cancelling the order at once- the answer is: no; not before further investigation.

Science service-
12.	Plant protection, $431,540,
Has the department done any investigational work recently respecting root rot in wheat?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture) :
speechtext: Investigations are being carried on continuously,, but I have not heard of any new development.

Those of us who were bom on the farm and received our early education there have never lost our interest in the experimental aspect of farm work. We have found that some of the greatest wonders of the world are on the farm. Last fall I witnessed gardeners planting brown bulbs in black earth. The bulbs have been frozen and thawed, and frozen and thawed again. It would do any expert in agriculture good to observe the floral beauty displayed to-day in front of these parliament buildings. It is magnificent. If hon. members taking part in the debate would see those flowers, which are more gorgeously clothed than Solomon in all his glory, they would be a little more appreciative of the work done, not only by the gardeners around this building, but by the Minister of Agriculture.

Now that the war is over I understand there is likely to be a much greater importation of bulbs and plants of all kinds into Canada. What measures are being taken to see that they are free from disease? I understand that in certain sections of Canada the production of bulbs and plants has become an important industry. I am told that in British Columbia the industry has been developed to a considerable extent. Are the products from that province being inspected so that there will be no danger of any plant diseases being spread to other provinces?

All regulations which applied prior to the war, and any which were added during the war, are being enforced. We are increasing inspection staffs to see that regulations in connection with the importation of bulbs and other plants into Canada are enforced. During the war the production not only of bulbs but of different kinds of seeds and plant life was developed to a considerable extent in British Columbia. Up to the present time new importations coming into Canada since the war have not affected that industry,

Supply-Agriculture

but attention is being given to the fact that the industry has been developed, and that care should be taken to maintain it.

Do I understand that before importations are made they must have a certificate of health? Or are they not inspected until they enter the country, with the result that they may have to be returned or destroyed?

It is not always possible to obtain certificates of health. On entering the country they are inspected carefully. Hon. members might be interested if I were to place on record the following regulations with regard to the importation of nursery stock:
Nursery stock includes all plants, or parts thereof, for ornamental purposes, propagation, or cropping.
1.	(a) A permit must be procured by the importer from the secretary, destructive insect and pest act advisory board.
' (b) The importer is required to advise the exporter of the permit number. This number must be marked upon the containers and shipping papers. (In the case of importations by parcel post, a special label is issued.)
(c) The permit must be presented to the customs by the importer when clearing the shipment. The invoice must conform with the permit as to kinds and quantity of plants.
2.	(a) Shipments must be accompanied by a certificate of inspection listing the kind and quantity of plants contained in the shipment and certifying them as apparently free from insect pests or plant diseases.
(b) Importations are subject to re-inspection on arrival in Canada.
3.	(a) Importations may only enter through one of the following ports: Halifax. N.S.: Saint John, N.B.; Montreal. P.Q.: (Quebec. P.Q., subport) ; Ottawa, Ont.; Toronto. Ont. (parcel post only); Niagara Palls, Ont.; Windsor, Ont.; London, Ont.; Winnipeg, Man.; Estevan, Sask.; Vancouver, B.C. (Victoria, B.C. sub-port).
(b) On arrival at a port, a shipment is either inspected immediately or permitted to proceed to destination for inspection on the premises of the importer:	It may not be moved from the
port unless either a "Certificate of inspection" or a "certificate of clearance" has been issued to the customs.

Some of the countries from which these importations come were overrun by the enemjq and perhaps the same care has not been taken to see that the plants are in healthy condition, or that plants which are infected are culled out. I do not think the minister answered my question whether bulbs and nursery stock from British Columbia require a certificate of health before shipment from that province.
The answer to the last question is yes; they must be inspected out there before shipment.

I understand that small parcels of potatoes are coming here from countries against which there is an embargo. They

are being brought in by people returning from Europe. What is being done to stop this procedure?

Anything of that nature brought in by immigrants is subject to inspection. All motorcars crossing the boundary line are treated in the same way. Seeds of any kind which are brought in, whether of potatoes or of anything else, are inspected. Aeroplanes, too, are subject to inspection. Of course I presume some people make an effort to avoid the inspection, but every effort is made to see that they do not.

I notice an increase of about 400 per cent in the equipment required by the division this year, and an increase in travelling expenses of about 60 per cent. In looking over the public accounts for last year covering this particular division I notice that a number of new cars and used motorcycles were purchased, after deducting an allowance of $300 for one used car. The public accounts show that last year two used cars were turned back at $565. Perhaps the minister could explain these two items, and at the same time indicate what travelling allowances are permitted to members of this and other divisions. I do not think the minister was quite right when he said last night that the car mileage allowance for employees who used their own cars was at the rate of nine cents per mile. I looked up the order in council which was passed last year just before the election, and I found that except for British Columbia the amount allowed for car mileage is nine cents per mile for 4,000 miles. I assume that is what the minister meant last night. After
4,000	miles has been travelled by a car, the rate is eight cents per mile. It seems to me that that is an adequate mileage allowance. Could the minister indicate what equipment is being purchased, particularly cars, and the nature of the discounts allowed? I think we are not getting a sufficient allowance on our used cars, unless they are actually in very bad shape.

The provision for paying for the operation of a car is on the basis of nine cents per mile. The rate was seven cents until the beginning of the war and for some time into the war, but it was found impossible to get men to drive their own cars because of the difficulty of getting cars and the extra cost of maintenance; therefore the basic rate was raised to nine cents per mile for the first 4,000 miles, and when a car covered a greater mileage than that, the rate was lowered.

Supply-A griculture
With regard to looking up the records having to do with car purchases and finding why more was allowed on one car than on another, I may say that our cars are all rather old and badly worn at the moment, because we could not buy any new ones after 1942; at least it was not easy to buy them. Incidentally I might mention that this was one of the most difficult votes to get past the treasury board. The amount to be paid is established in this manner: We call for tenders, usually from three different dealers.
Do you call in the dealers?

Suppose it is in Yorkton; they would ask two dealers in Yorkton and one dealer outside of that community to bid, and the best bid would be accepted. A dealer may say, "I will allow you $300 for your old car and charge you so much in addition for the new car." Another dealer may look the car over and say that he will allow a little more. Three bids are required under normal circumstances. During the war period it was not always possible to carry on in that way, and it is not yet, because often a dealer has no cars, or if he has cars, they are covered by permits already in his hands. The practice has not been established definitely for the whole area of transactions, but that is the practice followed to establish the value of the car.
How much equipment is being purchased under this $28,000?
There are about twelve cars, and then equipment of other type which will be used in the plants associated with this work.
The department bought four new cars last year and twelve new ones during the current year.
We have not got them yet, although we have the money to buy them.	.

The hon. member for Lambton West (Mr. Murphy) is not here, but he spoke to me about a matter which I should like to bring to the attention of the minister. It concerns a disease which is affecting the sugar beets in that hon. member's constituency.
.Speaking on this matter last year he explained that certain of the streams running into lake Huron were filling up at their mouths, causing a flooding of certain areas used for the production of sugar beets. The suggestion was made that something should be done by cooperation between the dominion and provincial governments and the municipalities. Has the minister any report to make on this matter?
63260-103J

The sugar beet nematode has been present in the sugar beet area of south western Ontario for several years, but the infestation is still confined to a restricted area centering on Blackwell in Lambton county. The crop losses, however, have increased within this area. In 1945 cabbages and cauliflower grown in infested fields were severely damaged by this nematode.
Experiments in soil fumigation to control the sugar beet nematode were repeated in 1945. The results of these experiments indicated that some of the commercial fumigants greatly reduced but did not eliminate the nematodes. However, the results indicated a sufficient control to treble the yield. No satisfactory method of control is known at present and as a result every possible field sanitary precaution is taken to prevent the spread of the nematode. It is also advised that farmers use a rotation which keeps sugar beets or other host plants out of known infested fields for at least five years. Experiments with soil fumigants will be repeated in 1946, using better methods of applying the fumigants over larger acreages.
I understand that a drastic method is adopted to- deal with this disease-sugar beets are not marketable off a field affected by nematode. The cooperation with the province is continuing.

Is there any suggestion that the provinces and the municipalities are going to share with the dominion the cost of opening up the mouths of these streams so that they will not flood and carry the fungus into the beet fields?

I remember there was some discussion about that last year but I am told that there has been no arrangement made to that end. I assume that means they are not convinced that that is the difficulty. I would imagine if they were convinced that that was the real cause of the spread of this disease, some action of the kind would be taken.
I understand that the municipalities are willing to go ahead and that the provincial government would do their share if they could get the consent and cooperation of the federal department.

I will look into that. I would imagine that if our people through their experimental work are convinced that that is a solution or at all events a help the matter would be considered; but possibly in carrying on their investigations they do not agree with those who contend that this would be a cure or assist in the cure.
Supply-Agriculture

What has been the experience of the department in using sprays to kill weeds in standing crops? What effect have the sprays had in killing the weeds, and what effect have they had on the standing crops? We have all seen display advertisements that these sprays can be used to kill weeds in standing crops without effects detrimental to the crop.
I can give more information on that w-hen we reach the item for experimental farms and Doctor Archibald is here.	*

Reference has been
made to cars. In view of the scarcity of cars has the department bought any used cars from War Assets Corporation?
We have bought very few. As a matter of fact we prefer to buy new cars, for obvious reasons.
On page 85 of the details there is an item, insignificant in amount, $1,500, for rent and taxes, but a principle is involved which prompts me to ask, what taxes does the dominion government pay?

We pay taxes on only one plant, and that is a fumigation plant in the city of Vancouver which belongs to the railway. The court has ruled that we must pay taxes on it. I cannot go into the details, but the court ruled that we had to pay the taxes, and the estimates provide for that.

Item agreed to.
Experimental farms service-
IS. Experimental farms service administration, $70,755.

I am glad to see an increase in the vote for the experimental farms service. The vote was cut during the war, and while there might be some justification for reducing it in war time, I think now is the time' to increase it. What I am going to say bears generally on the experimental farms service.
If we look over the salary schedules as shown in the details we are struck by the fact that the salaries still remain at a very modest level. Under "Administration" I notice that there are only four salaries over $3,000 a year, and if you look through the entire list of positions in services which I regard as very important, such as prairie reclamation, you will find that the same thing holds good. While we must do all we can to prevent any extravagances in the government service, I feel that generally speaking the salary schedules of our civil service are too low to
attract into the service the people we should attract. I am not derogating in the slightest from the qualifications of those already in the service, because I know from personal experience that some of them have remained in the service in spite of attractive offers to better themselves in private employ.
In the period we are entering a scientific approach to all our problems, including those of agriculture, is essential, and we should do everything we can to encourage young men to come into and remain in the public service and devote their lives to improving, for instance, our agricultural products. When wre look back over the years we begin to realize how great a contribution has been made by science to agriculture. Think of the contribution that one scientist made to western Canada, Doctor Saunders. In some material the other day I discovered that while, he was actually working on marquis wheat he was getting a salary of $100 a month. We have improved a little on that; nevertheless we should encourage the minister to do all he can to make these services-experimental farms, prairie reclamation, branch farms and so forth-sufficiently attractive to induce the best qualified people to enter the service.
The schedules reveal that the salaries are still comparatively low. Seven or eight years ago they may have appeared to be moderately attractive, but many hon. members know the high salaries that are being offered to-day by private industry to attract well-qualified young scientists.
The minister has said on one or two occasions that after all, these men are serving agriculture, that the returns to the man actually working on the land have never been very high, and that.the salaries paid to those in the agriculture service must not be very far out of line with the returns the farmer is getting. While there is some merit in that, I do not think it is really a sound argument. I would say rather that we must so stabilize the prices of agricultural products as to give the farmer reasonable returns upon which much higher salary schedules for agricultural scientists can be based.
I should like to say a word now, if I may, on item 16, as I tnay be called out of the chamber in a few minutes. This item, like many others, contains the phrase "notwithstanding anything contained in the Civil Service Act." I do not know just what that means, but again may I say to the minister that he or somebody else has been keeping many of our younger scientists on the temporary staff when in my opinion they should have been made permanent. I do not know

Supply-Agriculture
just how far that practice has gone. I have not been in close touch with Saskatoon lately, but I do know that a group of young men who were engaged there a year or two ago on the scientific soil surveys were still on the temporary staff at exceedingly low salaries, although it is admitted that- they have done magnificent work for our provinces. The very fact that the new assessment has been largely based on the soil surveys and has proven so satisfactory to the people of the province is a tribute to the value of the work that these young men have done. I am very anxious indeed to see that the civil service is a real civil service, and I should like to see temporary positions occupied by qualified men on a temporary basis made permanent and brought under the Civil Service Act, with appointments, so far as possible, made in the usual way by the civil serivoe commission.
But I rose to suggest that we should endeavour to support the minister in any attempt he may make to attract to our public service, particularly our agricultural service, the very best qualified young agricultural scientists who are coming out of the faculties of agriculture in our Canadian universities.
If I might clear up one point just made by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, I have never compared the salaries paid to scientists with the wages or returns in the farming communities.
I did not quite mean that.

No, but I just wanted that made clear. Every time we discuss the experimental farms service the question of labour on the farms comes up. Take for example the one that we both know best- Indian Head. There are people who live in Indian Head and labour on the farm whenever they can get work, some of them all year round, some of them a number of months out of the year.
I intended to mention that.

These men are paid on a basis which has some relationship to farm labour in the surrounding community, because they really do farm work in the fields which is the same as is done by others who are working around, I think the pay is usually higher than that for other farm labour, but not sufficiently high to make everyone want to work there.
What is the hourly rate there now? It used to be 25 cents.
It was around 35 cents, but I understand it has been put up 13 cents, which increases it to around 48 cents.
That is better.

I think that will tend to draw labour to the farm. At the present time,
I imagine, wages just about as high are being paid on farms round about for certain types of work.
On the other question, relating to scientists, a number of considerations enter into the matter of the pay. One, of course, is the ability of the individual, which in a service such as the civil service cannot be given the same consideration as an industrialist would give to it. We are governed by the rulings of the civil service commission, which must be more or less standardized. Industry is not affected by that kind of thing. I have not looked into the subject sufficiently to know whether the United States system of hiring persons is governed as closely by civil service regulations as ours is, but they do not seem to have more leeway in bidding for the services of highly qualified scientists.
This year, as I have said, on one or two occasions we have insisted that, under regulations last year which came into effect on April 1st of last year, these payments should be reviewed throughout the departments. As I said the other night, we are getting along with the job more rapidly than most departments, but we are not satisfied that all the increases which ought to be made have yet been made. We agree that we should pay these men just as much as we can pay them in relation to the costs which are being put against the people generally in order to meet their obligations. Having said that, I think I should add that there are many people who would rather work for the government than for anybody else.
No, no.
Somebody says, "no, no". I do not happen to be one of these myself.
You have been doing it a long time.

But I find that every time we ask that a position be filled a great many people want the opportunity to fill it. I can understand that. They come under the civil service; they are guaranteed employment, provided they apply themselves to their work, until they are sixty-five, and then they have superannuation. In industry one is very fortunate, in certain lines, if one can stay beyond forty or forty-five. Superannuation allowances or similar compensation may be provided, but after all, people like to work as well as to get money for working. A scientist does. He likes to work, and he would like to be sure that he will work until sixty-five.
Supply-A griculture

He does not want to stop at forty-five and hang around the rest of his life. I can understand that type of individual wanting to work for the government and being prepared to work, having these guarantees, for a little lower return. Whether we should ask them to accept these salaries or not, there are so many of them ready to do this work and trying to do it that there is more difficulty than one might imagine in raising the salary level when dealing with public funds.

Regarding this matter of agricultural scientists, when the minister's estimates were up last year I put on the record a chart showing what scientists in similar employments in industry and other services received in Canada, the United States and Great Britain. X am sorry to say that what our men received was considerably less than the pay for analogous positions in the United States and Groat Britain. It may have some relation to what has also been stated here, namely that agricultural producers in Canada receive censiderably less than the producers in either the United States or Great Britain. However, as I said then, and has been said by the Iron, member for Rosetown-Biggar, our farmers can scarcely estimate in dollars and cents what some scientists have done for them in the production of rust-resistant wheats and other things of the kind; and I just want to put in a plug for the minister in getting better remuneration for these agricultural scientists whenever the opportunity presents itself, because occasionally, I am sorry to say, we lose good scientists to these other countries. While they like the work, they are human enough to want to be paid for it, and sometimes they cannot resist the offers of high remuneration which come from other countries. Now and then we lose an outstanding man because we do not pay him sufficient money. I believe anyone who studies this situation at all will be quite satisfied, to see ,this class of civil servants paid the worth of their hire.
Will the minister state what has been done recently in the matter of developing newer types of rust-resistant wheat, both the hard variety and the durum varieties? What are the newest types of wheat and their possibilities, so for as the department can say now?

There are only two new varieties of wheat which have been developed recently and are ready for release. One is hard spring Renown, which is a rust-resistant wheat, and the other is the Rescue wheat, which is sawfly resistant. Experiments are being carried on in the developing of Durum,

and of other hard wheats which are rust-resistant, but they are not ready for release -and on the soft wheats, too.

What about the
Carlton? Is it sufficiently recognized as rust-resistant?

No, it is not ready for
release. It is being experimented with.

I know I shall be
forgiven if I bring to the attention of the committee a question which has been agitating our section of the country for quite a while. I do not feel very diffident about it, because the minister will realize that ever since I have been in the house this, is the first time I have asked a question on his estimates.
I want to mention a position which is now open, the superintendency of the experimental farm at Kapuskasing. Before proceeding any further I want to pay a tribute, and in doing so I believe I am voicing the opinions of every section of our population, to the retiring superintendent, Mr. Smith Ballantyne, that fine, big, Nova Scotian' who, after living for forty years in our section, has become a real northern Ontarian. He has done real work in his position and he will be greatly missed. Everyone concerned must compliment the Ontario government upon having caught Smith Ballantine on the rebound and giyen him a fine position in northern Ontario in connection with agricultural and colonization operations, for which he is well qualified.
I think that the deputy-minister knows our position well; in fact, that he realizes the situation as well as I do, because he has done us the honour of visiting our section of the country and that particular farm on many occasions. When the La Ferme experimental farm in Quebec, which is adjacent to our own section in nprthem Ontario was closed around 1934, more work was put on the shoulders of the experimental farm in Kapuskasing. That is why in replacing the man who had carried on that work there for many years in a satisfactory manner, certain regional and racial considerations had to be taken into account.
The experimental farm at Kapuskasing is serving an agricultural population of almost three quarters of a million people. In my own section, the Cochrane district, we have had the greatest development in colonization and agriculture in Canada in the last two decades. If you visited northern Quebec in the Abitibi, Pontiac and Chapleau districts you would also see one of the greatest agricultural movements, second only to the one that was experienced in the three western provinces. On its

I want the committee fully to realize our situation. Because of that I know the committee will realize the logic of my request. That is all I want to say on this subject. I must say here that I leave it entirely in the hands of the department, which has been fair to the agricultural population of my district so far as departmental activities are concerned. However, I do make a serious request, namely, that the man to whom I have just referred and who is well known to the deputy minister and the minister himself, a man who is well qualified, a man who will be a loss to Quebec if he leaves that position to come to our province, should be given consideration. Would the minister tell us what proportion of the total allotment for experimental work the Lethbridge farm is receiving? What is the nature of the work being carried on?
The hon. member for Acadia raised the question of weed control. The idea I have in mind is a little different from his. I should like to know what the experimental farm at Lethbridge is doing in connection with weed control. A serious situation is developing in my constituency. Within the last few years four exceedingly serious weeds have come into that area

They are: the leafy spurge, the field bindweed, the hoary cress and the Russian knapweed. They could be a menace to the whole of western Canada if they ever got completely out of control. If work on the control of these weeds is being carried on, would the minister tell us about it? Would he tell us whether in the judgment of the men responsible there is adequate machinery available to the Lethbridge experimental farm for the carrying on of a study of the control of these weeds? Have they sufficient staff? Is there enough money to give the staff the hired help which they need in order to accomplish the desired results? What is being done in this connection at the Dalroy substation of the Lethbridge experimental farm?

Weed control work is done at the substation in question. The amount spent at Lethbridge, out of the votes which are being discussed, is 878.790. There is, I understand, about another 880,000 which comes under item 16, which' has some relationship
["Mr. Gardiner.]
to the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Aot, but the total amount here is 878,790. Weed control also comes under item 16, and I do not know that there is any reason why I should not say, under administration, ini connection with all these votes, that weed control by the methods indicated a few moments ago is being carried out on the different experimental farms. As I have said, work is being done at the substation just mentioned, under the control of' Lethbridge, and there is also work at Indian Head and other experimental stations. The treatment is a very successful one. I said yesterday that I had had the privilege of noting the work which is being done at Indian Head. The road from my farm to Regina leads past that station and I drive by it continuously. I did so last summer and was more than surprised to find how successfully you could spray a field. They sprayed one strip and- left another strip unsprAyed. A field that was infested with mustard was sprayed and the mustard was entirely killed, while in the field which was not sprayed the mustard was there as before. The peculiar thing about it was that the ground seemed to be better after it had been sprayed than the ground which had not been sprayed.
Is it expensive?
About $2.50 an acre. It is apparently a successful mothod of dealing with mustard at least and, I assume, with other weeds such as the stinkweed, what we call the French weed.

The point of greatest importance to us is that these four weeds are deep-rooted perennials Which have peculiar habits of growth that make it next to impossible to kill them with the devices that kill ordinary weeds such as stinkweed and mustard. The men in my constituency used to think that they had real trouble when they were faced with the Canada thistle and with the perennial sow thistle. They thought they had reached the climax when they had to cope with those weeds, but they decided that, in comparison with their experience with these four new weeds, they did not know what weeds were. I am wondering if any kind of chemical control has been discovered which is effective against these four weeds. If a chemical remedy has not been found, has some method of culture or of crop rotation, been discovered, which has a chance of being successfully applied against these weeds?

Experimental work is being done to obtain a chemical which can be used against these four weeds, but it has not progressed sufficiently far for the depart-

ment to recommend or to guarantee it. They are still working on it, with a view to obtaining a chemical which will accomplish the same thing as the chemical now produced does accomplish in connection with mustard, and the hope is that they will be successful. There are cultural methods of dealing with all kinds of weeds, and they have cultural methods for dealing with these particular varieties. How successful they will be is a matter that depends upon those who. are applying the cultural methods, but the farm at Lethbridge can give those in that community the best information that can be had with regard to the. matter. Unfortunately I do not know whether the experimental farm at Lethbridge is treated by the neighbours in the same manner as some other farms I know of. It seems that those who live closest to a farm pay the least attention to it in many cases. People will drive many miles to go to a farm to look it over, to see what can be done, but those who live in proximity to that farm think it the natural thing to drive by without stopping to investigate. That is what they usually do. However, if people go and make inquiries at Lethbridge with regard to the experimental work being done there they will get the latest information available with respect to the handling of these weeds.

My chief concern in bringing this matter to the minister's attention is this. We may not realize how serious the situation is and for that reason we may not be giving the Lethbridge farm the amount of money which they require to conduct their experiments against these weeds and to push them to a successful conclusion. Let me indicate how serious the situation is. The leafy spurge has tap roots which often reach from ten to fifteen feet under the ground. Any man who has any agricultural experience will realize that it is impossible to reach the roots of a weed that goes so deep down. The roots run horizontally at from four to eight inches under the ground, and from these creeping roots come up new plants. Anyone knows that if these roots run eight inches under ground they are entirely below the reach of ordinary cultivation. It starts growing so early that smother crops are not effective against it. I am sure that all hon. members from Saskatchewan and Manitoba realize how serious is the threat to their own provinces if such weeds get thoroughly going in Alberta, with west winds blowing over that province.
Then consider the field bindweed. It ha? a root system which is quite extensive and which may penetrate to a depth of twenty feet. Roots of bindweed plants have been
known to spread six feet outward and five feet deep in fourteen weeks after the seed germinates. Before we saw this weed in action in my constituency we would not have believed that any such plant existed, but we know now that it does. Then there is the hoary cress. The roots have been found thirty feet deep. Mature plants send running roots out at different depths beneath the surface, some of which are far below the depth of cultivation. It is exceedingly difficult to eradicate them in slightly alkali lands. Thus it is a menace to our whole area. We have four irrigation projects in our constituency, and wherever there is irrigation there tends to be some alkali development. It is proposed in that region to have a conservation project which wild bring under water 350,000 more acres. Hon. members can see therefore how serious the situation is with weeds like these spreading into those areas. They cannot be eradicated by any method which the farmers so far have discovered.
The Russian knapweed is a perennial, propagated by seeds and by running root stalks, and it is almost impossible for the smother crops to cope with it. One of the reasons why these weeds are so difficult for the smother crops is that they start growing so early in the spring that they fill the ground completely with roots.
I think I have said enough to impress upon the committee the gravity of the problem. It is not a fly by night affair; it is a potential menace to the whole nation. I urge the committee to support the minister in expending whatever money is necessary to cope effectively with this weed problem while it is still in the infant stages. It is only scattered here and there in small patches at the present time. I am told that in some places in the United States this weed has really got a thorough hold on the ground, that in those areas the cost of eradication is as great as the total value of the land, and that it has become impossible to get loans on land infested with it. Certainly no hon. member wants to see anything like that established in Canada.

I support what the hon. member for Lethbridge has said. We already have this weed in Manitoba. The dominion experimental farm, in cooperation with the provincial departments of agriculture, is doing good work in experimentation. In fact they have a chemical they have been using for some years which leads us to the belief that the development of the weed can be controlled. We have not experimented long enough to have direct proof, but good

work is being done, and certainly I can substantiate everything the hon. member has said about the seriousness of leafy spurge. When I served on a municipal council we found that the cost of keeping it down and preventing its spread was greater than the original value of the land.

For a number of years at the experimental farm at Fredericton experiments have been carried on in connection with a blight-resistant potato. Have any of these potatoes been released for planting? If not, why not? I understand some good varieties have been developed.

We have been experimenting with about twenty varieties, but they are not yet ready for release. This means that we are not ready to say that we are certain we have accomplished what we set out to accomplish. However, the experiments do give promise.

Recently in Ontario, and I expect in other provinces as well, there has been a revival of what are known as permanent grass mixtures. Experiments are being carried on by the federal experimental farm, by provincial experimental farms and by individuals. Recently Mr. Fraleigh of Lamb-ton, a pioneer in this work, died. He did good work in the development of grass mixtures of different kinds for permanent pastures. What is being done by the central experimental farm and by other federal farms in this connection?
Mr. TOWNLEY-SMITH: Would the minister tell us the present situation in connection with Rescue wheat? This wheat was developed comparatively recently, and has proved more ar less resistant to damage from sawfly. May I speak first about the mixed grasses for pasture purposes. As the hon. member for Haldimand knows, the mixtures are not the same in all communities. We are carrying on experimental work, based on the work formerly done by Mr. Fraleigh. That work is being carried on successfully at different experimental farms across the country.
Western members will know that sawfly did not do a great deal of damage for some years in western Canada. Gradually the damage has increased to the point where in some areas it is almost impossible to grow wheat. One might say that that has been the history of growing wheat. Wheat growing, as I recall its history in this country, started down on the little island at the mouth of the St. Croix river. They could grow whealt there, and the growing of it extended across Canada. I can remember that when I was a boy on a farm in Ontario the only kind of spring wheat grown there was Goose wheat. My grandfather and my father used to tell me that they grew nothing but spring wheat when they went there first. There came a time when they could not grow it, because of certain things that had happened in connection with the growing of it. Wheat growing on this continent has moved gradually westward and northward. Wheat, like another plant we mentioned a few minutes ago, is subject to certain diseases and insect attacks. If the growing of it is overdone, if we crop wheat year after year with very little rotation, we

eventually build up the pests which attack the plant. If this is continued, we may be driven out of wheat in some areas.
Without the experimental work that has been done in connection with rust, probably by this time we would have been almost out of wheat production on the prairies. Our crops were wiped out so many years in succession that we simply had to stop trying to grow wheat at all. Had it not been for the finding of rust-resistant varieties, our corps would have been greatly reduced. We find that when wheat such as Thatcher is grown continuously in one area, the rust-resistant qualities decrease. We thought it was one hundred per cent rust-resistant over great areas when we began growing it, but I think to-day it is rated at about sixty-five per cent. It is just possible that, by being grown over and over again, varieties may get back to a position where they are not resistant to some attacks. Therefore the experimental farms keep working at their job all the time, and continue to develop new varieties which will resist different kinds of rust.
The sawfly is another thing which is being dealt with. This is the insect that cuts off your wheat, and by the time you are ready to harvest it, it has harvested it for you and there is nothing you can do about it. The department has been working on the production of a sawfly resistant wheat and has produced one variety which is able to resist the sawfly fairly successfully. This has been distributed earlier than it otherwise would have been because of the great damage that has been done by the sawfly. It is not a variety which will stand up against grading to produce the top grades. I am not in position to indicate all that it lacks, but baking and other tests which have been made show that it is not capable of being placed in the top grades, and it would not be fair to the consuming public to have it placed in those grades. It must be graded down because it does not produce the results that the higher grades of wheat will produce. This does not mean that we cannot get a wheat which will be sawfly resistant as well as being a top grade variety. The work being done is in an effort to obtain wheat which will be sawfly resistant and rust resistant, give a good yield and grade good quality all the time. When such a wheat is obtained it will be classified along with the others. In the meantime we are carrying on with the investigation and experimentation.

This is one of the best branches of the whole department, and in this connection I should like to say a word or two about four of the experimental farms that I have seen in the last two or three years.
The Indian Head farm is carrying on a wonderful work in the production of shade and other trees for distribution throughout the west. The head of that farm gave me the figures of this distribution, but I have forgotten them. If they were put on Hansard I am sure they would be found to be quite formidable.
I should like to refer to the work being carried on at the Swift Current farm in the development of new machinery. One man there who apparently has a mechanical turn of mind showed me many machines which had been developed at that station and which had demonstrated great value.
That would be Mr. Denike.

The distribution of
trees by Indian Head has been going on for many years. There are two forestry farms in Saskatchewan, one at Indian Head and one at Sutherland, near Saskatoon. I have not separate figures for the two farms, but we did distribute from six to ten million trees from the two farms. These trees have been distributed free of cost but they must be planted under regulations set by the farms. The farmers who got those trees have taken great care to follow the instructions. I happen to have a farm where the tree planting was done by the farmer who had the farm before I had it; I bought the farm with this work already done. The former owner had no special knowledge about growing trees but he took instructions from Indian Head and planted the trees as they told him to plant them. The trees now make a very fine windbreak around the buildings. Many of them have been there since near the beginning of the century. Trees have been distributed from that time on, and earlier than that, now all over the western country. The nurseries themselves have brought up the question occasionally and have insisted that the -work be carried on. One might think that the nurseries might object to it, but when the matter was fully dis-

cussed they have always agreed that this distribution of trees induced so many people to want to have shrubs and trees around that it helped the business of the nurseries, because once people had learned to grow a certain type of tree, it led to them purchasing other kinds.
The work carried on in the west with regard to apples started at Morden, which is the centre from which it all radiates. When I first went west in 1901 I was living sixty miles from Morden. Everyone talked about the place. When you went by Morden on the train you would always see a case of apples on the station platform during the apple harvest season. They were a very nice appearing variety of apple, and most people got off the train to look at them. The idea of growing apples in the west has spread from there all across the prairies.
On the map, Beaver Lodge seems to be quite a distance north of Morden, but when I first went up into the area represented by the hon. member for Peace River I was astounded to find them growing there the type of grass crops grown in Ontario. They actually were seeding timothy and clover, which we did not seed in Saskatchewan or in southern Manitoba. If one is familiar with the growth around Morden and then goes up to Beaver Lodge and takes a look at the growth there, one finds much the same crops growing there as at Morden. In other words, the climate of the western country runs along a line which >
parallels the Rocky mountains almost all the way across the prairies. If you draw one line down the height of the mountains and then go fifty miles inland and draw another line paralleling the first, generally speaking the climate follows that line. But there is this variation; the height of the mountains in the north is lower than to the south and the warmer winds get farther in from the Pacific. This warmer climate brings about a growth in the north to the west such as you find in Ontario. Eor that reason the plants first developed at Morden have been transplanted to Beaver Lodge farm. It was first operated by the late Mr. Albright himself on his own farm before we took it over. He had an illustration station and worked on it and developed it himself with the assistance and help of the officials who would call in to advise and help him. Throughout his life he did a great work for agriculture in that area. The farm is now operated by the department; the trees have been transplanted from Morden to Beaver Lodge and sent out to illustration stations over the whole area, and many people are now growing fruit trees, particularly apple' trees, in that area.

Would the minister say a word about machinery?

I had intended to do so. I am quite sure that if the farmers of Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Alberta would write to the experimental farm at Stvift Current before they bought farm implements, they would save far more money than they would lose by the 12^ per cent increase in the price of implements. There are many implements purchased in western Canada which the farmer is better off without. An agent persuades him to buy some implement on which very little experimental work has been done. The farmer buys it and uses it one season and then throws it into a fence corner, if he has a fence. That expense could be saved if they would only write to the experimental station when they think of buying any new implement. I have always worked on the principle myself on my own farm that as long as an implement is doing a job all right I do not buy another kind of implement. I was out at the experimental farm at Swift Current two or three years ago and I took a walk down along the end of the plots where they are experimenting with different kinds of equipment. They had all the newest equipment that is put out-combine seeders, combine harvesters, and the rest. But what I was most interested in was the plots which deihonstrated that you got the best results with the old-fashioned plough and the old-fashioned harrow and cultivator and the old-fashioned seed drill. I looked at the plots as I walked along the end, and I saw that it was these old-fashioned implements which produced the best results, I went home quite satisfied that I had not bought many of these new-fangled implements which are put out to save a great deal of money and do so many things for us.
On a number of occasions I have discussed with the director, as he will remember, the advisablity of our putting out publications
saying what we think. There is some danger in that too. We find that when we put out statements saying what we think, the farmers sometimes do just the opposite-even if it has to do with summer-fallowing. You get the best results when the farmers go to the experimental farm and see the results for themselves. Some take advice a little more readily because they feel they had something to do with discovering the truth of it. But if you try to drive them into doing a thing, not only do you meet with opposition from the man who has bought one of these new implements and thinks it is doing a good job, but there are also the implement companies who can send out more agents to tell the opposite story to the one we can tell with the money that is voted to us. So we hesitate to start any controversy. I say again that if every farmer will go to these experimental farms and look at the experiments which are being carried on, he will be able to judge for himself and save himself a great deal of money on his farm.

We have to have a certain kind of implement suited to a certain kind of soil. Using the old implements on certain kinds of soil did not succeed very well in western Canada. Try using a disc and harrow on sandy soil, and you will get into plenty of trouble. Many farmers in the west had to discard those implements and use some of the new-fangled ones. The tiller to use in spring time brings the best results in my part of the country. You have to pick certain implements to suit your type of soil, in just the same way that you choose certain varieties of wheat and other grains to suit the soil and locality in which you are farming.

I am looking for a little information. Recently I had a conversation with one of the old country millers, and the story he told me caused me a good deal of worry. He said that the old country small bakers are pretty well passing out of the picture, and that the large mills are building huge bakeries to produce bread on a mass production basis. His claim was that our western wheat, while the very best for the -small baker, rises too fast and is a little too hard to control in these modern bakeries, and they are now asking Canada to produce wheat which is not as fast, wheat which has more gluten and less protein. Has the minister any information on that?

I do not know whether it is the same miller or not, but a miller of the Scottish Cooperative was in this country during last winter. I had discussed the matter with him in Glasgow in January, before he came to Canada, and I also discussed it with him later here in Ottawa. The idea which has been mentioned by the hon. member is much as he stated it to me, and I assume that what he says is correct, because he is one of the leading millers of Great Britain. Throughout the years the Scottish Cooperative has used a larger percentage of our wheat in their milling than any other mills in Great

Britain. As a matter of fact, prior to the world war they were using 100 per cent of our wheat in all their best bread. They used other wheats for other purposes, but for bread-making flours they used 100 per cent of our wheat. They were doing that in 1936 when I was over there, and other mills at that time in England were using 30 to 40 per cent. When a miller of that kind, a man who has been associated with a milling organization which prefers to use all our wheat, and advocates doing so even now, calls our attention to the fact that a change is probably taking place in methods of baking in Britain which will require a little different type of wheat, I think we should pay some attention to it, and I am quite sure that the officials of the department will be paying attention to it.

What information has the department regarding the progress of studies of bacterial wilt in alfalfa? My information is that so rapidly has this pest progressed in the alfalfa fields in my area that numbers of fields are almost completely out of production. I am told that the Lethbridge experimental farm is devoting a good deal of attention to this problem and that if it is not making all the progress which is desired this is probably because it is not receiving enough financial support. Could the minister tell the committee what is being done at the Lethbridge experimental farm to meet this condition, who are the men who are particularly working on the investigation of bacterial wilt in alfalfa, and whether he feels they are adequately paid and equipped?

The men who are investigating bacterial wilt in alfalfa are really engaged in a branch that we have just passed, that is the science branch. The work which is being done on experimental farms is associated with trying to evade the results by selecting seed carefully and then by not planting on the same ground too soon after the wilt has appeared there in any year.. In other words, it is being done through rotation of crop and seed selection in so far as the farmers are concerned, and I am informed that in so far as it is necessary to do that work in connection with experimental farms the men are there and the money is available too.
I might say that in a number of these matters hon. members have raised questions about, we have no difficulty in getting the funds which we have in these estimates for those particular purposes. The question which arises each time we come along is, "Well, how much can you efficiently spend during the

You would probably say in answer to that that if we pay enough salary we will-get the men. Maybe we would. I would not be too sure about that. At the moment our main difficulty with all these matters is getting a type of technical staff which can deal with the problems that are there, and as far as we are able to get the men to put on the work we have been able to get the funds to deal with it.

May I say, in addition to what the minister has said, that while this problem of bacterial wdlt in alfalfa does not of course assume anything like the proportions of the problem I raised a few moments ago with regard to those four kinds of weeds, nevertheless this problem is a serious one in that area, because alfalfa is commonly raised at present as one of the series of crop rotation plants which are used in connection with sugar beet culture. Therefore everything that can possibly be done to discover an effective way of controlling bacterial wilt should be done as soon as possible. I am told that one of the projects they are following is to develop a new type. I understand that Grimm alfalfa is the type commonly used iin the area, but that it is believed by certain alfalfa scientists that an entirely new kind should be developed in a manner similar to that in which have been developed new kinds of wheat, namely, rust-resistant and sawfly resistant wheat.

I was remarking to the director here, as the hon. gentleman was speaking, that the last time I was in Lillooet I thought they had one of the finest experimental stations I had seen anywhere operated by an individual. I have forgotten his name; I believe it was MacMillan or some such name. plot which in the old days produced all the wheat consumed in that area. My experience has been that I produce enough in my own garden, and with veay little labour, to supply my own, requirements and those of my immediate neighbours.

I was surprised by the growth of raspberries. From what I had read my thought had always been that there was some difficulty in .growing raspberries in a garden. May I on behalf of my constituency express the appreciation of our people for the Lethbridge experimental farm. The minister has indicated that in some instances the people who live around an experimental farm do not appreciate its efforts, but that is not the case with respect to the Lethbridge farm. This farm has taken a leading position for many years in the advancement of agriculture. One important problem with which it had to deal was that of soil drifting, and the device of strip farming, with which the minister is familiar, was developed and introduced by the Lethbridge experimental farm. That has proved to be of great value to the district.
Ever since I can remember, this farm has been under capable management, and it still is. I think it is only fair to the earnest civil servants who have devoted their lives so unselfishly to the welfare of the people that something should be said about their efforts and I take this opportunity of expressing our appreciation.
I urge that this experimental farm be given more and more support as the days go by. As I stated in my previous remarks, this farm is located in an area which offers many problems. It must be prepared to deal with problems arising from the great irrigation projects. There are two sugar beet factories and three outstanding canning factories located in the district. It must deal with such problems as coordinating the activities of the man who raises cattle in what is known as the short-grass cattle country with the activities of the feeders in the beet growing areas and those of the stock raisers up on the Milk river ridge. Men there are raising stock under entirely different conditions from those faced in other parts of the country.
The officials of the Lethbridge experimental farm have never needed to be told about any particular problem; my experience has been that they are always ready to reach out and take a lead.
There are some problems that will still require a good deal of investigation. One is the clutivation of sugar beets. As the Minister of Labour and the Minister of Agriculture both know, it is becoming increasinglj7 difficult to get men to work in the sugar beet areas. Machinery will have to be developed to do this work, and the Lethbridge experimental farm is taking a lead in this connection. I shall not go into detail, but they are developing machinery to handle such operations as loading, planting and cultivating. These machines have been carefully tested and developed and information given out to the farmers, and the farmers have received this gratefully. The Lethbridge experimental farm has cooperated in every way with the officials of the sugar beet factories in the development of this machinery.
There is another problem that exists in the southern part of my riding. It has been found quite feasible to raise certain small fruits and the Lethbridge farm has taken the lead in this connection. They have taken different strains of small fruits and have sought to develop strains that would be suitable for the area.
I have no wish to multiply words by going into too many details, but I want to close by saying that the work of this farm has been deeply appreciated. I commend the minister for the manner in which he has supported this farm. If he will increase the amount of money for this purpose he will have our support.

Yes,, I understand that. The minister's remarks yesterday were very much closer to the matter. He said, as reported in Hansard, at page 1593:
. . . unless the promise of crop conditions changes materially within the next month we are not going to be concerned so much about finding markets for our farm products as we shall be concerned about feeding the live stock we have.
These remarks are becoming truer every day, especially in the district I live in. This matter is of urgent importance right now, taking into account all things in connection with it. For instance, telegraphic crop reports of the dominion bureau of statistics dated May 14 show precipitation since April 1 below normal, Manitoba 38 per cent, Saskatchewan 41 per cent, Alberta 61 per cent. The same crop reports from Swift Current areas indicate that conditions have deteriorated owing to the dry, windy weather. Soil drifting has reduced the stand on isolated fields throughout that area. Many areas report that recent heavy frosts, in some districts as low as twenty-six degrees, have damaged early-sown grain, particularly barley. The full extent of damage cannot be determined owing to the early spring. Pastures showed good growth but are now turning brown in some districts.
My experience is that a week after the grass starts to turn brown it is bad for grain. This is the 17th of May; the season is getting pretty well on; and I think we should not leave it further to chance. Conditions could be much worse this year than they were, even

in 1937. In that event we should be sure that enough seed and feed are kept in the west to take care of requirements for 1947 in the different districts affected. It would be the height of folly to have to ship grain back to those areas that are affected.
The wheat pool summary for the week ended May 10 states that the heavy frosts which were experienced throughout Saskatchewan have resulted in injury to all crops which were appearing above ground and that, because of the continued high winds, which in some areas reached a velocity of fifty miles an hour, damage by soil drifting has, of course, steadily increased, the condition has grown worse, and a period of calmer weather is urgently needed.
Because of the foregoing, seeding has stopped and the acreage is nine per cent, or
1.186.000	acres, lower than the "intentions to plant estimate as at April 30, 1947" issued by the dominion bureau of statistics.
A further report from the Canadian grain statistics, week ended May 2, 1946, shows
12.250.000	bushels of wheat in country elevators in Saskatchewan. Divide this between the 3,500 elevators and it works out to about 3,500 bushels to each elevator, which is very low indeed. And, now that there is a speed-up in shipments in Europe, this amount may be less. I note that the amount of wheat purchased by the farmers in 1937 through the government was over six million bushels. This is more than half the amount of wheat that is in the elevators of Saskatchewan to-day. Again I would urge the government to give this important matter its earliest possible consideration. If wheat has to be held because of crop failure, the government should see-to it that prices will not be higher to the farmer than they are now for other domestic needs.

speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, I believe the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) was speaking when the debate was adjourned.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. MacKINNON (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
subtopic: COMMISSIONS TO AGENTS IN CONNECTION WITH SALES OP WHEAT
speechtext:
Last Friday evening, Mr. Speaker, I had time to make only a comment or two on the bill introduced by the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Fair). I mentioned that I considered it would be unwise to pass this bill in its present form, and that I thought the bill should receive considerably more discussion and attention before being further'dealt with. I also stated that in my opinion the bill went farther than the hon. member actually intended it should go.
I do not wish to take up much of the time of the house this evening, but I should like to review briefly the operations of the Canadian wheat board in relation to the bill now before the house.
In discussing this bill, it may perhaps be advisable if I begin by recalling the circumstances under which the Canadian Wheat Board Act was established in 1935. Canada faced an acute wheat problem in 1935 and the Canadian wheat board act was passed by the Conservative government of that year. The subsection which the hon. member for Battle River now desires to have removed from the wheat board act has been retained without change since the act first was established. In other words, this subsection has been the policy of both the Liberal and Conservative parties.
The subsection of the wheat board act of which the hon. member for Battle River is critical reads as follows:
In selling and disposing of wheat as by this act provided, to utilize and employ without discrimination such marketing agencies, including commission merchants, brokers, elevator-men, exporters and other persons engaged in or operating facilities for the selling and handling of wheat as the board in its discretion may determine.
Instead, the hon. member for Battle River proposes that the board should:
In selling and disposing of wheat as by this act provided, to employ such methods, consistent with the provisions of paragraph (b) of this section, as will not involve the payment, directly or indirectly, of any commission or other remuneration to commission merchants, brokers and other marketing agencies.
May I point out one or two of the basic differences between the new clause and the original provisions contained in the wheat board act. The existing section of the act authorizes the Canadian wheat board to employ the usual marketing agencies, notably the elevator companies and the grain exporting firms. The effect of the new regulation, should it be carried into force, would be to prevent any of these agencies from being employed by the board since it no longer would be possible to have any commission or any other remuneration paid to them.
It should be remembered that the Canadian wheat board has already dispensed with futures brokers under the War Measures Act by P.C. 7942 of October 12, 1943, which closed the wheat futures market.
This suggested new bill would go even further as a matter of permanent policy and do away with the services of the elevator companies and the grain exporters.
Passage of this bill would prevent the Canadian wheat board from having the power to pay any handling charge to the elevator companies, including the three western pool organizations which, I imagine, would be put out of business.
I am quite satisfied that the hon. member for Battle River, in introducing this bill, did not anticipate or did not support any such move. But, actually, the bill as before the house would mean just that.
I would like to suggest that careful consideration should be given to any measure which would have these results.
When the Canadian wheat board, as at present constituted, was being debated in this house in 1935, the importance of wheat to the prosperity of the Canadian people was stressed in all parts of the house. Perhaps I may be allowed at this point to sum up some of the main arguments used in that important debate so that we can have this material as a necessary background to our deliberations.
It was pointed out that Canada is the largest exporter of wheat in the world. In 1935 production was greater in both the United States and Russia. Russia has produced as much as one billion bushels of wheat per year. As a matter of fact, I think that figure is very
Canadian Wheat Board

conservative. I believe Russia has produced up to 1,600 million bushels of wheat in a single year. The United States has produced many average crops in excess of SOQ million bushels. Both these figures are, of course, larger than the annual yield of the Canadian wheat crop. But all the same the fact cannot be denied that Canada is the largest exporter of wheat, and we are, therefore, primarily concerned in suitable markets and the orderly sale of our wheat on the world market. I may point out that these objectives are included among the primary duties of the Canadian wheat board.
During the disturbed economic conditions which prevailed in the 1930's the marketing of Canadian wheat faced many difficult problems. Many European countries which had formerly been good customers of Canada at that time, embarked upon a policy of economic nationalism. They built tariff walls to shut out our wheat and other products, and bonused their agriculture in the vain attempt to grow selfsufficient in foodstuffs, though clear-minded students of the problem were aware that this policy could not be realized except at a heavy cost. Surpluses of wheat were accumulated in Canada during these disturbed years and it was at last clearly apparent that a new departure in policy had to be made.
May I remind the house for a moment that our experience in wheat in the 1920's had been very different from our experience in the 1930's. World conditions were much more satisfactory from Canada's view point in that period as a great exporting nation than they were in the latter period. The 1920's had witnessed the growth of the three western wheat pool organizations which were destined to play such a notable part in the wheat economy of Canada.
The pools had a clearly defined marketing policy in Canada. This policy consisted in paying their patrons an initial advance at the time of delivery and a subsequent payment when the wheat was finally marketed.
