speechtext:
Well, call them patrons or members. I will not quarrel with , the hon. member on that.
When the period in which the pools made their initial advances came to an end, the Conservative government from 1930 to 1935 embarked on a policy of buying wheat and holding it in order to support the market. No useful purpose would now be served by trying to measure the success or failure which attended this controversial policy. All of us can recall the arguments which were used on

both sides during this troubled period. But, in retrospect, this judgment can surely be pronounced, in all fairness, because it is based simply on the record of those times. Despite whatever motives may have inspired the policy of the government, prices for Canadian wheat continued to remain at low levels and the government accumulated wheat stocks which were much larger than it was the normal practice for this country to carry.
The situation became so disturbed that farmer organizations pressed their demands very strongly to have the Canadian government issue a guaranteed minimum advance to wheat producers, and the Canadian wheat board was created in 1935 for this as well as other reasons.
I would like to emphasize that as constituted in 1935, the wheat board was a voluntary organization as far as producers were concerned. Growers had a choice of delivering their wheat to the board and taking the initial advance from the government or of selling their wheat outright on the open market.
On October 12, 1943, the government passed an order in council, P.C. 7942, whereby the Canadian wheat board was changed from a voluntary board to a compulsory board in so far as producers' deliveries were concerned. Consequently, so long as the futures market remains closed, the Canadian wheat board necessarily remains the sole marketing agency for Canadian wheat. The wheat policy, with respect to the fixed initial price as announced by the government on September 27, 1943, and set forth in detail in this order in council, had five main points. First, it involved the discontinuance of trading in wheat futures in the Winnipeg grain exchange. Second, the Canadian wheat board acquired, on behalf of the dominion government, all stocks of unsold cash wheat in Canada on the basis of the closing prices which prevailed on September 27, 1943. Third, the fixed initial price was raised from 90 cents per bushel to $1.25 per bushel No. 1 northern wheat, basis in store Fort William-Port Arthur or Vancouver. Fourth, it involved the closing out of the 1940-41, 1941-42, and 1942-43 wheat board crop accounts, also on the basis of closing market prices as they existed on September 27, 1943. Fifth, it involved the use of government-owned wheat to meet requirements under mutual aid and to provide wheat for subsidized domestic purchasers. It will be evident to the house that the powers vested in the board under this order in council were far-reaching. The Canadian wheat board not only took over all unsold commercial wheat in Canada, but it also became the sole marketing agency to receive wheat from producers.

Canadian Wheat Board
It will be seen at once that the activities of the board have been greatly enlarged by this extension of its duties and responsibilities. A very great strain has been placed upon the whole organization in these war years. This strain has been particularly heavy upon its accounting staff.
I would like at this time to pay tribute to the work of the Canadian wheat board, to its commissioners and to its entire staff, with special reference to the advisory committee of the wheat board. I am in daily touch with the commissioners of the Canadian wheat board and I can testify to the abnormally heavy responsibilities which the board has been called upon to discharge, and I believe it has met these responsibilities with credit to itself and with satisfaction to the wheat producers and the people of Canada.
I am sure what I have said in this respect will receive the hearty endorsation of every hon. member who is at all familiar with the operations of the Canadian wheat board.
During the discussion in this house that followed my statement of September 19, in the last session, when I outlined the government's wheat policy in its main esentials for the next five years, I took occasion to explain that this statement of government policy made no reference to the continuation or non-continuation of the wheat board. I anticipate and the government anticipates that the Canadian wheat board will continue indefinitely.
It will not have escaped the attention of the members of this house that at different periods the Canadian wheat board, in the interests of wheat producers, has followed different policies with respect to marketing. This flexibility is one of the great assets of the system by which the Canadian wheat board conducts its extensive business. It might be a disservice to wheat producers to require the wheat board at the present time to cling to-some arbitrary and inflexible method which would not take into account changing circumstances of the world market together with changing conditions of world supply.
May I emphasize that prior to the war, countries which bought wheat from Canada almost exclusively obtained their wheat supplies through private importers who dealt with the grain exporting firms in Canada. Many believe that it would have been a mistake in policy at that time to confront these importers with a Canadian government monopoly selling agency.
I would like to emphasize once again that it is by no means clear at the present time whether the governments of other countries, which are now employing government purchasing agencies, are pursuing this policy 63260-104
merely as . an immediate aftermath of war conditions, or whether they hope to continue their monopoly import agencies. Until the policies of the import countries become more clearly defined, it may be that it would be a mistake on Canada's part to destroy the private trade in Canada. There are people who believe that a government agency can perform all the required services more cheaply than can private firms.
I know that the people who hold this view hold it very strongly, and that they are able to argue strongly in its favour. I would be the last person to deny the sincerity with which these views are maintained.
May I make it quite clear that I do not now propose to enter into a general debate on the virtues of a government agency versus a private firm. My whole argument has been directed toward the fact that this particular moment provides a very bad time in which to define our future policy with rigidity, without taking into account the buying methods to be followed in the future by importing countries, together with changing world conditions in wheat policy and wheat prices. If we have a free hand, we can then take advantage of changing circumstances and not be tied to a rigid policy which, if defined to-day, would mean that it has been defined in advance of more normal world conditions. I think that in suggesting that this house take this action and not run the risk of any premature decision on a matter of such fundamental policy, I will be urging the house to accept a policy which will commend itself to its good judgment.
Throughout the history of the Canadian wheat board the board has employed the facilities of the country elevator companies as agents for the board in taking delivery of producers' wheat. The board has also employed the grain exporting companies in making export sales of wheat under board authorization and in looking after all the details of getting the grain moved from the terminal elevators at the lake-head to eastern seaport positions for export. I would like to stress the fact that an alternative to the use of the country elevator companies and the grain exporting firms would be the expropriation or purchase of the physical facilities of these companies or the setting up of an expensive alternative service. The cost of their administration would have to be set against any savings in the commissions and handling charges that are now paid. It is, therefore, very difficult to ascertain what actual savings could be effected by this means for the benefit of producers.
I have spoken at this length in order to inform the house of some of the main purposes

Canadian Wheat Board

which the Canadian wheat board has sought to fulfil since it was created to deal with the difficult emergency problem in 1935. The wheat board has shown its ability to cope with our wheat problems in peace as in war. It has now built up a vast and valuable body of actual experience which will serve it in good stead in the years that lie ahead. I believe that the wheat policies of the government are well conceived and will advance the best interests of Canadian wheat producers. We enter a period of reconstruction in a sound position. We are free to shape our policy so that changing conditions in the world market can be quickly met. This freedom is a great asset and it should not be lost by any premature decision now on the use of marketing agencieg, such as must be involved in the bill now before the house.
The main point which I have tried to make in these remarks is that this motion does not relate exclusively to the operation of the futures market, but in reality concerns many questions affecting the welfare of Canadian farmers. These more general questions are very complicated and very important, and can most appropriately be considered by a committee which will be appointed to examine this whole matter in detail.
I move:
That this bill be not now read a second time but that the subject matter thereof be referred to the select standing committee on agriculture for consideration and report.

Nevertheless I do not feel qualified to vote intelligently on this bill as it stands; I feel I do not know enough about the subject to be able to give an intelligent vote. A considerable number of farmers to whom I have talked have attached the Winnipeg grain exchange vigorously. A considerable number of others, including the most successful and prosperous farmer I know, are all in favour of having the grain exchange continued. I think my position is similar to that of a large number, of other members. I wish to make it clear to-night, as I believe I made it definitely clear on other occasions, that I do not want to be a party to the weakening,of the wheat pools of western Canada, that I am not a supporter of the grain exchange, and that I want the wheat board to operate and handle all kinds of grain, not only wheat. On April 30 and May 7, when this bill was under discussion, I began to wonder whether I was some sort of criminal in view of the way the discussion ran on the other side of the house. I wish to point out that I was in favour of a wheat board for Canada at the end of the first great war, even then realizing that the board was created to hold the price of wheat

down rather than to send it up to inflated levels. I was one of those who supported the move to have the wheat board continued, and when we failed to persuade the government of the day to continue the board I was one of those who began organizing the Alberta wheat pool and helping in the best way I could similar organizations in the other provinces. I was one of the first farmers in my district to sign a wheat pool contract; I signed the first and second series; and since that time I have delivered practically 100 per cent of the grain I have grown to the wheat pool organization. I am still doing that. Perhaps that may clear up any misunderstanding which may exist at the present time as to where I stand in connection with the wheat pools and the wheat board organization. I believe the staff of the wheat board to-day is a very good one. I did not say that the other night; I did not think it was necessary because I felt that my stand was well known and did not require a Philadelphia lawyer to figure it out, as would be necessary to find out just what some other hon. members have been driving at in their speeches since the bill was introduced.
The hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Jutras) spoke in support of the wheat board, and I was very glad to hear him speak as he did, even though he ridiculed to a certain extent the stand I have taken in the framing of the wheat board amendment. Let me say that I am a farmer and proud of it, and that I did not myself try to frame that amendment; I went to a member of the legal profession to have it framed. Let me again make it clear that I have no objection whatever to any amendment of the bill which will bring about the results which I desire to have brought about, namely to put the Winnipeg grain exchange permanently out of operation. In his concluding remarks the hon. member for Provencher had this to say: Hansard, page 1292-I believe it places him definitely against the operation of the grain exchange:
All of which reminds us of the story of the buyer working for a group of millers who came west to watch the wheat markets. After a few days he wired his principals to this effect:
"Some think wheat will go down and some think it will go up. I think so, too. Whatever you do will be wrong. Act at once."
That describes accurately, I believe, the operations of the Winnipeg grain exchange as they affect the farmers of Canada. The little fellows who were and still are compelled to sell their grain during the first three or four months of the new crop year are the ones who suffer and pay the penalty of our keeping in operation the Winnipeg grain exchange.
Later in the debate, on May 7 we had an oration from the hon. member for Rosthern

(Mr. Tucker). He discussed this question with much more heat than light, and unless I interpret his remarks incorrectly, his speech was a conglomeration of contradictions. Here we have him getting things mixed up a little bit. First of all he had this to say: Hansard, page 1296:

DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE Production service-
17. Production service administration, $38,865. Mr. CASTLEDEN: I should like to ask a few questions regarding the production of hogs in Canada. A few years ago the government introduced a policy of paying the freight on all feed from western Canada to eastern Canada, and I believe the milling companies took advantage of this. We also paid the freight charges on the brans and ' shorts which they obtained in the milling of the grain into flour and mill feed. At that time it was of tremendous importance to have as much production as possible. The people working on the farms in the east required some assistance, I presume, in getting feeds, down where they could be used to feed hogs. Is the Canadian taxpayer going to continue to be put in the position where he shall have to pay the freight on feed from the west where it is grown to eastern Canada where it is fed, or will the grain be left in the west to be fed where it is grown? It is surely in the interest of economy to feed that grain in the west where it is grown. Does the minister intend to continue the policy that is already in force, or what are the plans with regard to it?

The suggestion was
made that the millers took advantage of the policy to do certain things. The policy itself was drafted in such a way that the part of the wheat which enters into the feeding of live stock was provided for along with other feed grain; and whoever may be shipping the feed east from western Canada, if that feed is to be paid for as part of the policy of maintaining prices, then the bran and shorts which are fed to live stock have to be paid for just the same as oats, barley or any other grain.
The policy was based in the first place on the idea that men in eastern Canada, as far east as the maritime provinces, did not get sufficient returns from the production of hogs at prices then obtaining even to pay the cost of production. I think every hon. member from the maritimes will agree that this contention on the part of the maritime farmers was true. I do not know whether every hon. member from the west thinks as I do in regard to these matters, but I think it is just as important that the farmer in the maritime provinces, in Quebec or in Ontario should be able to get his cost of production as it is that a farmer anywhere else should do so. For a long period the farmers of the maritime provinces have not been able to produce enough hogs or beef to feed themselves. Their production does not enter directly, though it may indirectly, into the trade which results in our sending very considerable quantities of beef and pork to Britain; but on balance there is always an importation of our meat products into the maritime provinces to help feed their population. So what we are really doing, and what we were at least asked to do before the war, was to assist in covering the enormous freight charges which must be paid on feed grain going from the western prairies to eastern Canada, particularly to the maritimes.	-
There is another way of accomplishing the same, end, and I must say it was the ^ other way that was advocated for a long period of years; that is, controlling freight rates downward to the point where it would be possible for grain to be shipped east. The position is that we have a lower freight rate on grain going directly through to Britain than on grain going to the maritime provinces. That is a part of our freight structure which is very well understood in this house. It was always contended that we should lower the freight rate to the level imposed on grain going directly overseas. That position I think was placed once or twice before what was then called the railway board, now the board of transport commissioners, and the question was argued out as to whether the freight rates should be reduced in that way. After ^ war broke out, however, we undertook to do it in another way, by paying the freight on the grain from Fort William east, and paying the freight on the grain from Calgary and Edmonton west to British Columbia, in order to make it possible for the prices board to maintain the price ceiling, at the same time making it possible for those on the farms to produce under the price ceiling. That is why the policy was established; and I suggest that the whole principle of controls is involved in what is
Supply-Agriculture

proposed here. To take the freight payments off grain, including bran and shorts, coming to eastern Canada would compel an increase in the prices of the products produced through the feeding of live stock, which in turn would involve increases in wages and everything involved in the price control set-up.
As to what we should do in western Canada, I have not figured it out exactly, but it is often said that we produce enough wheat to feed thirty million people, and we produce enough coarse grains to feed far more live stock than we can ever persuade western farmers to feed for any purposes. Unless we produce far more grain than we can ever persuade western farmers to feed, we can never get the total production of live stock in this country up to where it otherwise would be. After all, I think it is more essential that farmers, whether they live in the east or the west, should cooperate with one another than that we should talk a great deal about others not cooperating with us. If we are to expect cooperation from other sections of the population, then at least we must expect to cooperate among ourselves. I would not join in any criticism of the western farmer for growing feed grain which cannot possibly be grown in eastern Canada, in order to make it possible for eastern farmers to feed more hogs and produce more beef and dairy products. That is one way we are asked to cooperate in order to keep up production and make possible higher returns to the eastern farmers; it is not done to benefit the millers or any others, and I believe the taxpayers of Canada would agree that something should be done along this line. If we cannot persuade the farmers to do something of that kind in order to bring about cooperation and make this possible then I am afraid we are going to lose much of the cash return farmers right across Canada have been obtaining as a result of the policies that have been followed; and I would hope that representatives of rural seats in any part of Canada would not begin to advocate a policy of insisting that in the first place we grow only as much coarse grain as can be fed upon our farms, and in the second place that we should not cooperate fully in making it possible for farmers in other parts of Canada to produce to at least as good advantage as we can produce in the west.
I do not want the minister to put into my mouth words I did not say. I asked whether it was the intention of the government to continue the policy.
If you had just asked me that you would have been given a different answer.

I was also giving some facts; and the fact is that the farmer of the west will raise more hogs if it pays him to do so. It is a further fact that the production of hogs in western Canada has gone down to a far greater extent than the production of coarse grains has gone down. To-day the farmers of the west are dropping out of hog production to a tremendous extent, but you would get a very heavy production of hogs in the west if you would make it profitable for the farmer to raise them.

I have not found the farmers of western Canada opposed to the government paying freight on feed coming east in order that the farmers of eastern Canada may have a chance to feed some live stock. But the farmers of the west feel that if the eastern farmer is allowed the benefit of free freight on grains to be fed to his live stock, the farmer in the west should have the freight paid on his five stock when they are sent east, in order that the price on the Moose Jaw market, for instance, will be exactly the same as the price on the Toronto market. They think that would make it fair for the eastern farmer and make it possible for the western farmer to also produce some live stock. I think the farmer who grows feed grain in western Canada, and who wishes to feed it to his own hogs, should have an additional price paid to him to take care of the difference in the cost of his feed grain, as compared with the cost of a man in western Canada who is a feeder, and who can obtain grain in western Canada at from ten cents to twenty cents a bushel cheaper than can the farmer who has to consider the cost of his grain at the same figure as the elevator price.	*
A resolution was passed last January by the Saskatchewan agricultural society asking that the price of hogs be increased to the farmer who feeds his own grain to his hogs, to the extent of $3 per hog. If these things were done, then I think the farmer in western Canada would have an equal opportunity to [DOT] raise hogs and live stock, and get the same kind of benefit from the government's policy as to-day the eastern farmers are obtaining.

' This question has been under discussion a number of times, and probably this is a good time to say something which may result in our thinking a little more clearly with regard to it than sometimes we appear to do.
I believe if hon. members will examine the record they will find that the western farmer does do better than the eastern farmer. This suggestion so often made that the western farmer does not do as well as the eastern

Supply-Agriculture
farmer is not borne out by the facts. There are more farmers in eastern Canada than there are in western Canada; but if one takes the cash income of the farmers who live in the two sections of Canada he will find that, even in some of the most difficult years we had in western Canada, our returns per farmer were higher than were the returns per farmer in eastern Canada.
They have expenses, the same as we have. I have been operating a family-sized farm in Ontario for some years. I have also been operating one in Saskatchewan. They were both family-sized farms, the one in Saskatchewan being a half-section at that time, and the one in Ontario 150 acres. I took more off the Saskatchewan farm every year than I did off the Ontario farm. I interchanged the stock between the two farms in order to prove to my own satisfaction that it was not just the breed of hogs that I had out west that gave me more money. I produced the same type of hog out there that I did on the farm down east, and made just as much per hog in western Canada throughout the war-time period as I could make in eastern Canada.
I even went through the experience of shipping a carload of grain from western Canada, under these arrangements now being discussed. That carload of grain I grew on the farm out west, shipped it to the farm down east and fed it to live stock. Perhaps I should say I saw it fed, or that sometimes I saw it fed. Plowever, I did see some of it fed. I know, too, that the arrangements made by the government-and I know this from experience -put the farmer in the eastern part of Canada in the same position as if he had grown the grain in western Canada.
The arrangements were supposed to figure out in that way, and they actually worked out in that way, when the actual transaction is carried on of growing the grain on a farm in the west, shipping it to a farm in the east and feeding it to live stock in the east.
It is true that under our arrangement of paying the freight and giving other assistance, as we were doing at the time, one can lay grain down on the eastern farm and feed it there at just about the same cost as though he fed it back on the farm in Saskatchewan. That is what I tried to do, and that is the way it works out.
It was as a result of that that we got the production of live stock in Canada which we did get. The suggestion is made that if you pay a higher price for hogs you' should produce more of them. I would ask hon. members to go around and take a look into 63260-105
farmers' bins in Saskatchewan. You will find that some of them are carrying wheat-and that includes some persons who have been discussing wheat to-night. But you will find, too, that right on those same farms there is not much left in the way of oats and barley. Oats and barley are still being fed to hogs.
I am quite sure the leader of the C.C.F. party would not agree with some of the things said along these lines within the past few minutes, because he was most outspoken in his opinion that we ought to be sending more food to Europe. The only kind of food Europe is asking for at the present time is grain-and grain in greater quantities, particularly wheat.
No one will suggest that at this time, as we did two years ago, we ought to be feeding 90 million bushels of our wheat each year, and that we ought to be sending 150 million or 160 million more bushels of it to the United States to be fed. That was when they wanted meat in Europe.
But to-day they want wheat in Europe. As everyone knows, it takes about five pounds of wheat to produce a pound of pork. A pound of pork will not keep a man alive any longer than a pound of wheat. The result is that we are being asked not to fed wheat to hogs. Rather, we are being asked to send that wheat to Great Britain or to Europe.
We all agree with that.
If you agree with that, then agree with this, that with no wheat to feed, and with very little oats and barley to feed, you cannot have more hogs than before, no matter what the price is.
They are feeding more in the east.
Some of them. But would you suggest that we should have kept our feed out of the east?
No.

Well, then, the fact is that we are just feeding the same number of hogs in the east as we fed on an average before the war. In other words, we are just supplying the market we have always supplied, and we think we shall always be able to supply. We are growing feed grains in western Canada to sell them just as they are grown. If we can produce these goods to sell them, I do not think anyone out west wants to advocate a policy of feeding all coarse grains we grow in western Canada on our own farms. In the first place, we would not do it, so why advocate that policy?

Supply-Agriculture

Mr. TOWNLEY-SMITH: May I say a few words to demonstrate how this policy works out? I hope it will be considered straight thinking. When I grow barley on my farm in Saskatchewan and sell it to an elevator I get in the neighbourhood of fifty cents for the barley and fifteen cents for the bonus, making a total of sixty-five cents a bushel. Obviously, if I feed that barley to pigs on the farm I am feeding 65-cent barley. If, however, I have too much barley and I sell a carload of it to my farm friends in the east, they buy that barley for fifty cents a bushel, not sixty-five cents, because they have the freight paid, and because the bonus is paid to me as the grower, at the elevator, when my carload of barley is shipped.

They do not buy it at fifty cents.
Mr. TOWNLEY-SMITH: I am trying to feed pigs on 65-cent barley on my western farm, and I am 2,000 miles away from tidewater. My hog price on the Winnipeg market is about sixteen cents, and I enter into direct competition with my eastern friends who are right on tide-water and who are feeding their pigs on 50-cent barley.

No, that is not correct. The ceiling price is 64f cents at Fort William.
Mr. TOWNLEY-SMITH: How does it work out?

It is only the freight from Fort William east that is paid. But he pays 64J cents for barley. That is within one quarter of a cent of the figure you gave.
Mr. TOWNLEY-SMITH: Does that sixty-four cents not include freight?

A quarter cent ahead of your figure.
Mr. TOWNLEY-SMITH: The market in which he sells his hogs is a 19-cent market. Someone will correct me if I am wrong, but there is at least a two-cent spread between the price of his hogs and the price of mine, and there is a significant spread between the price of his feed and the price of my feed.

I agree with the hon. member who says that there should be some adjustment in the freight rates on feed which

existed before the war. It was an anomaly that we should have a freight rate structure in Canada that forced the farmers of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick to pay more for western oats and barley than was paid by feeders in Sweden and Denmark. That freight rate structure certainly created a hardship for feeders in Ontario, Quebec and the maritime provinces. I cannot quite agree with the prqsent policy of paying all the freight east of Fort William. The whole freight rate structure of Canada should be gone into thoroughly so that feeders in eastern Canada can obtain feed grown in western Canada at prices which will permit them to meet the competition of other countries which will be in the market in the very near future.
Three-quarters of Alberta, most of Manitoba and probably one-quarter of Saskatchewan have been trying to diversify their agriculture. The people in these areas felt that growing grain was not good enough. But this diversification is being killed by the present policy of the government. Statistics will show that hog production in Alberta, at least in the part of Saskatchewan that I represent, and in Manitoba has decreased in a much greater proportion than it has in Ontario, Quebec or the maritimes.
It went up more.

We wanted it to go up
more and it should have stayed up. The minister has defended that policy in this house for years and yet now he has turned around and is killing it.
I am still doing it on my farm and I am making money.

The general consensus in western Canada is that what the minister states is incorrect. He has had letters; I have had letters and other members from western Canada have had letters to that effect. I ask the minister to consider seriously putting into effect a policy which will maintain diversification in western Canada. It is absolutely necessary that we have a stabilized agriculture in eastern Canada. At the present time the eastern farmer is in a precarious position because the feed he is using is being obtained on a subsidized market. If the government continues to follow the policy which was outlined yesterday of cutting off these subsidies just as quickly as possible, the eastern farmer will find himself in a worse position than we are in in western Canada.

Since we are on thus item I should like to put on the record the very letter which came to me from the same individual.
It is not from the same individual.
It is the same kind of thing in any event.
It sets out what I maintain is in the minds of seventy-five per cent of the farmers in the area.

We will read it and see if we cannot learn something about it. This letter comes from a gentleman in Codette in the constituency of the hon. member for Melfort, and he sent it forward to me. It reads:
I am enclosing statement for hogs shipped and would you mind showing same to James Gardiner and ask him if he is shipping any from his farm and if he gets the same kind of a deal. All these hogs were pure bred and from the same sow.
Mine were all pure bred and from the same sow, as I mentioned last night.
I had been getting at least fifty per cent grade A before the price went up. I have sow and eleven young-pigs about three weeks old and I have a notion to knock them all on the head and sell the sow.
That is just about what the other fellow said; they must have got together.
I am feeding them seventy cent barley-
He is getting five cents more than my friend.

those that I am getting ready for market and if a farmer came to get barley from me he gets a rebate of fifteen or twenty cents.
Which he does not.
Why in heck don't those who feed their own barley get the same deal? No more hogs for me, to heck with them.
Fortunately he sent along his statement.
Mr. COLD WELL; How does he spell "heck"?

H-e-c-k. He had six hogs. There were no A's; there was one Bl, and five C's, or lights. He got $26 for the Bl, which shows it was not a very good one.
It was really lighter than he needed to feed as a Bl.
It was about the weight they are asking for.

Not what they are asking for, or he would have got more money. He received $114 for the other five, or about $23 each. As I said last night, I sent ten down and I got my statement just about the same -time as this one came in. Eight of mine were 63260-105J
A's and B's and I averaged $29. Two of them were heavies, and I averaged $32 on those. That is the answer to his question as to whether I sent any down and whether I got the same kind of treatment. Why did I get different treatment from what he got?
That is the question.
That is the question and it is easily answered. He had six hogs and, if the statement made by the hon. member for Melfort is correct, he is not short of feed grain.
It is not the same man.
The hon. member said that the farmers in his section of the country were not short of feed grain.
That is correct.
This is one of them. He is not short of feed grain, but he did not feed these hogs enough grain.
Because he was losing money.

He lost money because of the manner in which he fed them and sold them. The other man said that if he could get $32 for his hogs he could make money even at the prices which this man says barley is worth, which it is not. Barley is not worth anything like seventy cents a bushel; it is more nearly worth the amount the hon. member was speaking about a few moments ago.
It is worth seventy-one cents at the elevator.
On his farm it - is not worth seventy cents. It is worth what he would have to pay for it if he went to buy feed.
It is worth what he can get for it.

You can take it that way to serve your purpose. I know one or two men who were feeding hogs around Melfort. They were buying their feed, and you will find that they are paying just about the price that I am indicating for barley. If the man did not have the barley he could buy it for the price I am indicating and feed the hogs. Ontario is a typical mixed farming province, and in that province agriculture is an all-year-round operation. The picture on any farm in Ontario is one of costly buildings for the winter housing of all live stock.
Summer operations during the working season on a 100-acre farm would consist, probably, of a ten-acre field of wheat, a ten-acre field of oats or barley, a few acres of ensilage corn, perhaps two acres of roots of some kind, perhaps mangolds. In addition to the normal farm housing, the farmer must have a silo.
There is much work throughout the season taking care of the ensilage corn. There is the operation of cutting it, shredding it, and placing it in the silo, and a great amount of work throughout the winter in the feeding of it.
Then there is the use of wheat straw and oat straw in the bedding down of cattle, whether they be in open sheds or in stables. Taking it all in all, the Ontario farm offers an all-year-round occupation. That is what the farmer in Ontario expects to do. As a result of feeding operations, fertilizer is provided to go back on the land. This is an extremely necessary operation, and the only way in which the productivity of the farm can be maintained.
I have made this brief statement in order that hon. members may have a better understanding of the situation on a typical Ontario farm. It is quite different from that in western Canada where, in common practice, there is no labour in connection with keeping up the fertility of the soil. The land in the west is highly productive in its natural form.
I emphasize these factors as elements requiring the application of a great amount of labour, and involving a high cost of production. On these grounds it is only reasonable that the Ontario farmer should be given some little consideration by way of special rates on the additional quantities of grain he requires to finish his stock, and carry it through the winter.

When herds are placed under the government's Bang's disease policy the owners must employ veterinary practitioners to collect blood specimens. The first thing they must do is to employ a veterinarian to go out and take blood samples from the animals that may be afflicted with the disease. The blood tests are conducted free of charge at federal laboratories, of which there is one located at Lethbridge. When a herd passes three tests over a period of a year the department collects blood and conducts check tests. If it is negative the herd is listed for one year. That is, if they show that there is no disease for one year they are given certificates.	-
Licences for the manufacture of brucella abortus vaccine strain 19 are issued to approved Canadian laboratories. Hon. members will probably remember this as calfhood vaccine rather than under the official name. Import permits are issued to Canadian agents of responsible United States manufacturers and permits to purchase and use vaccine are issued to registered veterinarians. *
Adult cattle must not be vaccinated. They would probably remain positive to the agglutination test; consequently their export would be prohibited and they could not enter any clean herd. The use of vaccine during the calf age is supposed to prevent the disease later on, but the vaccine is not to be used on adult animals. When it is injected it causes the animal to be positive under test, and it would
not be permitted to enter the United States nor would any person purchase the animal for breeding purposes.

Doctor Duffy is at the Lethbridge laboratory and Doctor Allan is at Cardston.
Is it the intention of the government to pursue the same policy regarding tuberculosis free areas as was pursued prior to the war, or are they going to pursue a more vigorous policy?

It will be the same as
before the war, and we hope to get off to at least the same vigorous policy we were following prior to the war. We have not been able to get the men to do the work, although I have in my pocket a letter from an hon. member who says he has a veterinarian they are not using.
Will the conditions be the same as before?
Exactly the same.

I was going to pursue the matter of personnel for that sort of programme. I am glad to notice that there has been some improvement in the salaries being paid. Since coming here in 1940, I recall hearing that there were two or three veterinarians who were receiving less than $2,000 a year. Is any veteriniarian receiving less than $2,000 at the present time?
I understand not.

What guarantee has the purchaser of canned goods that he will get the same quality of goods according to the grade marked on the can in Ontario as he would in British Columbia? What supervision is there with regard to quality?

Can we leave that until we reach the marketing item?
Mr. TOWNLEY-SMITH: The other day, under the heading of "animal pathologists", I drew the attention of the minister to the fact that we are very short of veterinary surgeons, and he suggested that the subject be left over until we reached this item. I would repeat my question now. Will the minister not consider giving more encouragement to students in universities to take up veterinary science by way of offering scholarships and offering veterinary students work after they have. graduated ?	.
We have been giving consideration to this question but no policy has yet been worked out.

I am in emphatic agreement with what the hon. member for North Battleford has said, and in that connection may I read a paragraph from Maclean's Magazine from its "Cross Country" section. It says:
Prince Edward Island's 100,000 head of cattle have to share one doctor. So the province is scouting all Canada, to induce veterinarians to settle there. Premier J. Walter Jones, himself a farmer, estimated there is room for at least 10 veterinarians on the island.
The situation was forcibly brought to official notice when the milk and meat inspector of the city of Charlottetown died this spring. No veterinarian could be found to take his place. The situation might have been serious had not the provincial veterinarian, whose office and laboratory are in Charlottetown, offered to take the work.
I believe that statement to be essentially correct and, if it is, a serious situation exists. I would urge upon the minister to do everything in his power to alleviate that situation by following the suggestions made by the hon. member for North Battleford to accelerate courses and offer scholarships and inducements to students of veterinary science.

What are the annual requirements of the department through the retirement or death of veterinarians?
Mr. GiVRDINER: The normal wastage is between twenty-five and thirty a year, and we are not getting that number at present.

I wish to support what other hon. members have urged in this matter. The total number of graduate veterinarians from our colleges last year was at its lowest point, between twenty and twenty-five. It is important that the federal government in cooperation with the provincial government should face up to this problem. The Saskatchewan department of agriculture is offering a few scholarships. Since this is a matter in

Supply-Agriculture
which the federal government are also directly-interested, I think they should go along with the provincial government and match its payments dollar for dollar to see that this gap between the demand and supply is bridged.

At the last session of the house I drew the attention of the committee to the widespread prevalence of Bang's disease across Canada and to the fact that many people were becoming affected with undulant fever. The minister said at that time that when the estimates came up this year he would try to do something about the matter.
I again point out that the medical profession have still no cure for undulant fever. We have nothing whatever that will cure it. There is still no cure for Bang's disease, but we have prevention for Bang's disease, and that is calfhood vaccination. There is a list of casualties from undulant fever every year throughout this country, and the only means we have of controlling undulant fever is by calfhood vaccination. Our farmers are experiencing a great many losses of cattle through Bang's disease, and undulant fever is causing many casualties among human beings. The only measure of relief we have, and the only way of controlling undulant fever is by calfhood vaccination. There is no doubt that calfhood vaccination is really an effective remedy, but the trouble in Canada is that there is no unified effort because the regulations vary in each province. I will list the conditions in each province so far as Bang's disease is concerned.
In Ontario the work of controlling the disease has been placed directly under the Ontario agricultural college. An extensive programme of calf vaccination is under way, with strain 19, in an attempt to eradicate the disease from the province.
In Manitoba some funds are provided for vaccination of calves in pure bred herds by qualified veterinarians. -
In Saskatchewan there is calfhood vaccination, with Cotton's strain 19, for herds supplying milk to villages and towns without protection by pasteurization.
Alberta has also had calfhood vaccination since 1944, following a request from the western stock growers' association.
British Columbia has no special legislation.
In Quebec Bang's disease is controlled by the live stock sanitary law, and there are
5,000	listed herds, with 551 herds badly contaminated. For a- small fee owners of herds can have their herds tested under an agreement. The vaccination plan is used for contaminated herds.
Nova Scotia has no protective legislation. Many herd owners are doing their own vaccination.
Prince Edward Island has no legislation.
In New Brunswick there are restricted control areas, but there is a shortage of qualified veterinaries and inspectors to carry out the programme.
In regard to the efficacy of Cotton's strain 19 vaccine, I quote from the report of Doctor Welsh, director of the animal research division of Lederle Laboratories, Pearl River, New York, which is one of the largest laboratories in the United States. This article appeared in the Holstein-Friesian Journal of February of this year:
The recent report by Winter of New York state confirms the findings of others in that some vaccinated animals continue to show a positive blood reaction for many months after being vaccinated.
This should not be taken as a reason why calfhood vaccination should not be carried on, as he shows later. I continue the quotation:
His findings and others indicate that, on the average, calves vaccinated at the age of six months, give the best results. Calves vaccinated at four months of age or under usually do not establish a very high degree of resistance. Calves vaccinated at eight months or above retain their positive blood reaction for a prolonged time. The New York records, reported by Winter, on calfhood vaccination was in herds having 15 to 47 per cent infection. Of the animals vaccinated at six months of age, about 60 per cent were negative on blood tests six months later. At the twelfth month following vaccination, or when the animals were about eighteen months of age, at least 80 per cent of those vaccinated were negative and in some herds as many qs 90 per cent were negative. When these animals reached breeding age, they were bred, regardless of whether they showed a vaccination titer or were negative. Approximately 31 per cent of these animals vaccinated as calves were showing a positive blood reaction at two years of age but they found that the reaction receded during the first lactation period and that less than one per cent still remained positive at the time of the second freshening.
That would indicate that calfhood vaccination is effective. We should use any means at hand to control this disease.
As a physician I am concerned about undulant fever, and I as especially concerned over the apathy and listlessness with which this subject is approached by the department. This is the only cure we have. Something must be done. Therefore I say that calfhood vaccination should be compulsory on the strength of the records of the herds using it and on the strength of the records of the states where calfhood vaccination has been in vogue for some time. I think we can accept these records and particularly the record of the Ontario agricultural college, where Ontario is undertaking a mass programme. But if the different provinces have no set regulation, and it is done in a haphazard way in one province, contamination will be car-
Supply-Agriculture

ried from one province to the other by animals shipped from one province to the other. So tha-t the whole aflair, to be effective, must be dominion-wide, and I suggest to the minister, and repeat, that I am much concerned about the undulant fever, let alone the tremendous loss to the live stock owner, and feel that we must do something about the matter and make calfhood vaccination compulsory.

I greatly appreciate the contribution which the hon. member who has just taken his seat has made. My suggestion would be that the Minister of Agriculture for the dominion should call together in council the provincial ministers of agriculture; that this matter should be discussed and a definite policy arrived at which would be accepted by all the provinces, and that then there should be an immediate drive, which would produce results. In my opinion this disease has gone altogether too far to be reassuring.
Is the minister going to make a statement on this?

I should just like to join with the hon. member for Lethbridge in saying that the statement is a valuable one. A similar statement was made a year ago by the hon. member for Lanark, and I expressed my appreciation of it at the time. I quite agree with him that there is only one way by which we shall be able to attack the problem successfully, and that is by a policy somewhat similar to the one we have with regard to tuberculosis. We are not ready to proceed with it this year but it is being given consideration.

Has the minister
given thought to the possibility of publicizing this matter by radio broadcasts over the dominion, or has something of this sort been done? I doubt whether people in general understand sufficiently the seriousness of this problem.

I really think it is understood by those who are raising live stock, or the great majority of them; but, as has been emphasized this evening, it is just, three years ago since we accepted the calfhood vaccine. It has been used in the United States for some time, but our experts here did not officially accept it as a preventive until just three years ago. Since that time information with regard to it has been widely circulated. As a matter of fact, one of the reasons why it was officially accepted was that a great many people in Canada were writing in daily or weekly insisting on its being accepted, 
indicating that they knew something about it. Medical men, such as the hon. member who has just spoken to us, have been urging that something more be done about it than is being done, because, after all, as I understand it, this disease can be transferred to human beings-which is much more serious than the animal itself having the disease.
The same thing was true of tuberculosis. That is why we took such an active part in fighting tuberculosis; but there is an additional feature of it, that when I came here first, the first delegation I had in the department was a group of breeders from Ontario who were objecting strenuously to the e-xtent to which we were trying to regulate Bang's disease. As a matter of fact, they succeeded in having us undo some of what we had been doing. We were compelling any man who had undulant fever in his herd to stamp a big B on the cheek of the animal; but we were compelled by pressure to put the B in the ear, where it was harder to see. That was the attitude of persons who themselves were interested. We refused to make the B off altogether. The situation to-day is a little different. People have been educated up to the seriousness of the disease, just as a few years ago they were educated up to the seriousness of tuberculosis in cattle. I think we are getting nearer to the time when we can do something similar to what has been done with tuberculosis; but, again, it involves these larger staffs of veterinarians in order to put the policy in effect. Just as soon as we can see our way through it, some policy will be developed.

I have enjoyed very much the discussion which took place earlier this evening in which western members took part. I can only assure hon. members from the west that I personally was having a good laugh over it and I think most of the eastern farmers are good-natured enough not to have any ill-feeling as a result of some of the remarks which have been made.
Regarding the health of animals branch, I said certain things last fall which included some observations with regard to salaries in the civil service, mainly the health of animals branch, which branch I mentioned specifically.
I am glad to see there have been some changes in this department, not only in respect of salaries but in the reclassification of some of the inspectors. But I am doubtful whether sufficient has yet been done to get men to come into the service, and I am quite worried about the situation. After I talked to several of these boys, some of whom are in grades which have been reclassified, they wonder whether

Supply-Agriculture
it is worth while for them to remain in the minister's department. If they decide that it is not, and we lose more of the veterinarians now working in that branch, the situation will become that much more serious than it is. As matters stand to-day, I understand, according to the estimates, that there are still some men getting less than $2,400 who are working in this service. Is that so?
All the men who are now coming in are starting at $2,400.
I realize that is so, but I am asking the question, are there any in the service who are still getting less than $2,400?
I believe they are all getting not less than $2,400.

According to the estimates, there are a few who are still below $2,400. That is why I asked the question. It so happens that a man who joins the service now, starting at $2,400, could easily in four years rise to the same salary as a man who has been in the service for twelve or fourteen years. It would appear unfortunate that that is the case. I realize that ability must count. It is difficult for the civil service commission to get a true picture of what this whole salary schedule should be. But one thing definite in my mind is that men in the field, in charge of districts, who are doing as much and probably have as much responsibility as men in charge of packing plants, are not getting the salary that the man in charge of a packing plant is receiving. Personally I do not see any reason why there could not be some overlapping of the salary set-up which would give a stimulus to the man in the field who is performing this important service, so that he would have something to look forward to. As it is now, I believe the maximum for that particular grade would be $3,300.

Just to put the record straight, may I say that I understand the men in the field now do get as much as the men in the packing plants if they are in charge of' a district. That is under the new arrangement. What is being stated was true up until recently.
It has been quite recent?
Yes.
I am glad to hear it. It gives the man in the field an opportunity of going to $3,600.
Yes.

I am sure the men will appreciate that. I do not know for certain, but I have heard that the number who are
likely to come here from the veterinary college will not be over three or four. If that be the case, we cannot expect much increase in the work done by the health of animals branch for at least another year. In the meantime there are three counties in Ontario which have dropped back from the status of accredited areas. I hope hon. members will not criticize me for using Ontario figures and not the figures of other provinces. It is not that I am trying to differentiate, because I know the same will be true all across Canada. Three counties have lost the accredited area status, and one more county will lose it this year. The counties that have lost it are: Prince Edward, my own county of Brant, and the township of Pittsburg in Frontenac county; and Waterloo county will be out on August 1. The townships of Huntley, Fitzroy and Tor-bolton in Carleton county will be out on October 1. This is a serious situation. It is in tuberculosis alone. The w'ork of the past fifteen or twenty-five years will be put back a great many years if these counties are to be untested for just how long I am not sure. The infected animals will be left there to infect other animals, and this disease spreads quite rapidly. It spreads not only to cattle but also to other live stock, specifically hogs. Quite recently there have been several cases of hogs having to go to the tank because they were infected with T.B. But it is also transmissible to humans. That was mentioned by the hon. member for Lanark.
Bang's disease is probably just as serious as T.B., if not more so. Bang's disease is definitely transmissible to humans as the hon. member for Lanark said. So far the medical profession have found no cure for it. Neither have we a cure for Bang's disease in cattle. But as I mentioned in the house last fall, there is a good block or control for the disease in the form of brucella abortus vaccine, strain 19. Strain 19 is being used in Ontario to good advantage. A moment ago the minister made a statement that vaccine must not be used in adult animals. I ask him why that is so. I believe I proved to the house last fall that there were no ill effects from the vaccination of adult animals as found by the United States authorities with strain 19. It has been proven that even a cow that is near freshening can be vaccinated with strain 19. Probably she would abort, but that foetus can be exposed to any other animal in the herd, and, according to the United States report, those animals will not contract abortion. Therefore I ask the minister why-

The only reason I can give is that I must take my officials' advice
Supply-Agriculture

because I am not a veterinarian. My hon. friend is and he probably would disagree with them, but I must agree with my officials or- Mr. CHARLTON: I understand that perfectly. Probably some of the officials are still l^ack in the horse-and-buggy days. Surely we can take the results of the experiments in the United States as true. Surely we are not expected to carry on experiments of our own here and spend hundreds of thousands of dollars to do the same work they have done. The minister said that there is very little we can do without more help. I made another suggestion last fall with regard to the vaccination of calves to be raised in listed herds. I still make that suggestion. It is very important. I may say that it would take probably only fifteen minutes of the veterinarian's time when he is there testing the herd to try to tell the owner how important it was that he have these calves to be raised vaccinated. It would just be a matter of time; it would not be any extra labour. I venture to say that he would spend fifteen minutes talking to the farmer anyway, and it would be time spent to good advantage in explaining the situation to him.
I also said last fall that the listed herd is probably the most vulnerable of any herd in the country. Personally I would prefer to have the average herd on the back concession than I would the listed herd in so far as Bang's disease is concerned, because there is neither acquired nor natural immunity iSn the listed herd, and the disease can spread rapidly in that herd, much more so than in the average herd on the back concession. I have made two suggestions: first, that all calves to be raised in listed herds could quite easily be vaccinated. The vaccine is free; it does not take very long to inject it, and, as the hon. member for Lanark said, in only one and a half per cent of the cases were they still positive after the second lactation. Even though an animal is positive it affects it only for export. As a matter of fact, you might be a great deal safer to have an all-positive herd than an all-negative herd, if it was negative from the fact that it had not received the vaccine and was not infected. Personally I believe there are two things that could be done. The departmental officials should make themselves more fully acquainted with the system or draw in men from the United States who do know. I would suggest that they either communicate with the inspectors in the field who are doing the work or bring them in to a central point and give them a short course, explain the situation to them. There is one difficulty which should be cleared up in the minds of those who are vaccinating cattle.

Vaccine is not a cure; it was never supposed to be a cure, and the very thing that is probably worrying most veterinarians to-day more than anything else is that in many of these herds that have been vaccinated since 1936 or 1937-I will not say "many," but a few-abortions are occurring.
